summary: Psalm 10 begins with a direct question about why Yahweh seems distant in trouble. The poem then describes the wicked person’s arrogance, violent ambushes, and belief that God will not see or call him to account. It turns into a plea for Yahweh to act and ends by affirming that Yahweh hears the humble and judges for the fatherless and oppressed.
whyItMatters: This chapter gives readers a clear example of lament inside Psalms: it brings confusion about God’s hiddenness, detailed protest against injustice, and hope for judgment into one prayer. It belongs in Book I, where many poems voice distress and trust without pretending the distress is small.

context.author: Psalms is an anthology by many writers and collections; this chapter is not assigned here to a named author.
context.audience: Israel’s worshiping and instructed community, and later Jewish and Christian communities that adopted the Psalms for public prayer and private life.
context.date: Individual psalms may preserve material from the monarchy through the postexilic period; assigning one date to the whole Psalter would be misleading.
context.setting: Book I of Psalms, within a collection oriented around prayer, lament, praise, wisdom, and trust before God.
context.literaryForm: Compressed Hebrew poetry and prayer, here shaped as a lament that moves from complaint to accusation, petition, and confidence.

outline.heading: Questioning God’s Distance
outline.note: The speaker asks why Yahweh seems far away and hidden in trouble.

outline.heading: The Wicked Person’s Pride
outline.note: The wicked hunt the weak, boast, reject God from their thoughts, and imagine they cannot be shaken.

outline.heading: Words and Ambushes
outline.note: The poem describes cursing speech, secret violence, trapped victims, and the claim that God will never see.

outline.heading: Call for God to Act
outline.note: The speaker asks Yahweh to rise, remember the helpless, see the victim’s grief, and break the power of the wicked.

outline.heading: King, Judge, and Defender
outline.note: The ending affirms Yahweh’s kingship and says he hears the humble and judges for the fatherless and oppressed.

keyVerses.text: Why do you stand far off, Yahweh? Why do you hide yourself in times of trouble?
keyVerses.why: This opening gives the chapter its emotional problem: the speaker experiences trouble while God seems distant.

keyVerses.text: The wicked, in the pride of his face, has no room in his thoughts for God.
keyVerses.why: This line summarizes the chapter’s portrait of wickedness as arrogance that leaves no space for God’s authority.

keyVerses.text: But you do see trouble and grief. You consider it to take it into your hand. You help the victim and the fatherless.
keyVerses.why: This answers the claim that God does not see and names the vulnerable people at the center of the plea.

keyVerses.text: to judge the fatherless and the oppressed, that man who is of the earth may terrify no more.
keyVerses.why: The final verse states the hoped-for outcome: judgment that ends human terror against the vulnerable.

themes: judgment for the fatherless and oppressed

questions.question: Why does the chapter begin by asking why Yahweh is far away?
questions.answer: The opening is a complaint, not a calm statement about God’s absence. The speaker is praying from “times of trouble” and names the felt problem directly: Yahweh seems far off and hidden. The rest of the chapter shows why this feels urgent by describing the harm done by the wicked.

questions.question: Who are “the wicked” in this chapter?
questions.answer: The chapter portrays the wicked as arrogant people who hunt the weak, boast in their cravings, bless greed, and push God out of their thoughts. It does not give a personal name or a single historical setting. The figure works as a poetic portrait of predatory wrongdoing.

questions.question: Does the chapter say the wicked are successful?
questions.answer: Yes, verse 5 says, “His ways are prosperous at all times,” and verse 6 shows him claiming that he will not be shaken. The chapter presents this as part of the scandal: wrongdoing appears secure while the weak suffer. The speaker does not treat that success as proof that the wicked are right.

questions.question: Why does the poem spend so much time describing ambushes and traps?
questions.answer: Verses 8-10 make the danger concrete. The wicked person is pictured as lying in wait, murdering the innocent, catching the helpless, and crushing them by strength. The images show predation, secrecy, and unequal power rather than a fair conflict.

questions.question: What does the wicked person believe about God?
questions.answer: The wicked person says in his heart that God has forgotten, hidden his face, and will never see it. Verse 13 adds that he says God will not call him into account. The chapter presents this as a false confidence, because verse 14 directly answers that God does see trouble and grief.

questions.question: What does “Break the arm of the wicked” mean in this prayer?
questions.answer: The line asks God to end the wicked person’s power to harm. It is forceful judgment language, and readers differ on how such prayers should be used later: some emphasize handing vengeance to God, while others struggle with the severity of the wording. In this chapter, the request is tied to defending the helpless, victim, fatherless, and oppressed.

questions.question: What changes at verse 16?
questions.answer: The poem moves from urgent petition to confidence in Yahweh’s kingship. Verse 16 says Yahweh is King forever and ever, and verses 17-18 say he hears the humble and judges the fatherless and oppressed. The trouble has not been narrated as solved, but the prayer ends with trust that God hears and judges.

questions.question: Who are the “fatherless” and “oppressed” in the last verse?
questions.answer: The chapter names vulnerable people several ways: the weak, helpless, innocent, victim, fatherless, humble, and oppressed. “Fatherless” points to people without ordinary family protection, while “oppressed” names people crushed by others’ power. The chapter’s final hope is that God’s judgment will make such people no longer terrified.

glossary.def: The divine name used in this translation; in this chapter Yahweh is addressed directly in complaint and petition and affirmed as King.
The chapter’s repeated label for the arrogant wrongdoer who harms the weak and assumes God will not call him to account.
A repeated term for those targeted by the wicked and remembered by God in the speaker’s plea.
A vulnerable group named in verses 14 and 18 as people God helps and judges for.
